Chapter 1 Introduction The Quickomics tool can be accessed via the link https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com. Implemented through R Shiny, it helps with visualizing statistical analysis results for RNAseq and Proteomics datasets. This supplemental tutorial provides a detailed guide on using the different functionalities and customizing the tools to best fit individual analysis and plotting needs, using published RNAseq dataset and proteomics dataset as examples (Gyoneva et al., 2019; Connor-Robson et al., 2019). The interface contains multiple tabs, corresponding to different functional modules, that can be accessed on top panel of the webpage. Users have the option to upload their own dataset or choose from existing demo datasets for visualization. 1.1 Integrated Gene Set Query To supply genes in pre-defined gene sets to plotting functions in Quickomics, we developed xGenesets API for Quickomics to query and retrieve a list of genes/proteins when it is needed. The lists can be defined based on pathways, and gene sets from various sources, including KEGG Pathways (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000), WikiPathways (Martens et al., 2020), Small Molecule Pathway Database (Frolkis et al., 2010), Reactome (Jassal et al., 2020), Gene Ontology (The Gene Ontology Consortium, 2019), Molecular Signatures (Subramanian et al., 2005; Liberzon et al., 2015), and LIPID MAPS Proteome Database (Cotter et al., 2006). xGenesets database currently has 175,537 gene sets stored in MySQL tables, covering human (115,497 records), mouse (30,554 records) and rat (29,486 records) gene sets. xGenesets features personalized settings, dynamic drop-down list upon typing for quick gene set selection, full gene set database browsing, and a list of genes from any gene sets. Throughout Quickomics, users interact with this convenient tool in appropriate interface when a gene set is needed by checking “Geneset” option and then clicking on “Select Geneset” to pick a set from a table of available gene sets in a popup window as shown in the following screenshot. For developers of web-based applications (general user can skip this paragraph), xGenesets can be easily embedded in any modern websites and online applications, e.g., R Shiny web apps, by leveraging jQuery, DataTables, and bootstrap (either v3 or v4) JavaScript libraries. xGenesets API is freely available for all usages. Examples of using xGenesets API and guidance on setting up the API in your own applications can be found at https://bxaf.net/genesets. 1.2 Load projects from different data sources Besides selecting a project in the Dataset module or uploading files, a project can be opened directly with a URL. The part of the URL after ? tells Quickomics where to find the project. Quickomics can read project files from folders on the server, or fetch the same projects through the QuickOmics API, a separate service that serves project data. When the project loads, a message names the data source, and the source is also shown on the “Project Overview” page of the Dataset module. URL Where the project is loaded from ?datalake=ProjectID The data lake, through the QuickOmics API ?api_serverfile=ProjectID Published projects, through the QuickOmics API ?serverfile=ProjectID Files in server_dir, read directly ?api_testfile=ProjectID Unpublished projects, through the QuickOmics API ?testfile=ProjectID Files in test_dir, read directly ?unlisted=ProjectID Files in the unlisted/ folder of the Quickomics folder ?auto=ProjectID Tries the sources above in this order and opens the first one that has the project For example, https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com/?auto=ProjectID (replace quickomics.bxgenomics.com with your own instance URL). ?auto= is the easiest choice when you do not know where a project is stored: the data lake has the highest priority, then published projects (through the API, then read directly), then unpublished projects (through the API, then read directly), and finally the unlisted folder. If the project is found nowhere, a message lists the sources that were tried. When a session is saved with “Save Session” (Section 15.2), Quickomics records the source the project actually came from, so the restored session opens the same data. Projects stored as files on the server 1. Prepare the files for each project: projectID.RData, projectID_network.RData and projectID.csv. A wgcna_projectID.RData file with pre-computed WGCNA results can be added as well. The csv file should have four columns: Name,ShortName,ProjectID,Species Two optional columns for the csv file include: ExpressionUnit (you can enter something like log2(TPM+0.1)), and Path (optional path for raw or analyzed data, e.g. Z:/share/GSE158470/). 2. Put the files in a folder that Quickomics reads. The simplest way is the unlisted/ folder under the Quickomics folder (?unlisted=ProjectID). A better way is to keep the data outside the Quickomics folder: create a config.csv file under the Quickomics folder, for example: category,value server_dir,/hpc/data/server_files test_dir,/hpc/data/test_files Make sure the two folders can be read by the Shiny App. Files in server_dir are opened with ?serverfile=ProjectID and files in test_dir with ?testfile=ProjectID. Projects served by the QuickOmics API The datalake, api_serverfile and api_testfile sources need a running QuickOmics API. Its address and login are set on the server in the .Renviron file of the Quickomics folder (QUICKOMICS_API_URL, QUICKOMICS_API_USERNAME and QUICKOMICS_API_PASSWORD). If the API cannot be reached, opening a project from one of these sources shows an error, while ?auto= skips them and continues with the next source. 1.3 ShinyOne Starting from Quickomics v2.0, we also introduce ShinyOne, a web-based table listing existing projects loaded into Quickomics. We have pre-loaded several demo data to Quickomics, and the ShinyOne demo site is: http://demo.bxgenomics.com:8185/

Chapter 2 Dataset Module This first module is for selecting dataset. Users can either select from pre-loaded example datasets or upload their own dataset in a pre-defined format as detailed in section 2.1 and in our GitHub page (https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics). We have pre-loaded four datasets from published studies that users can use for demonstrative purposes. These includes two RNAseq datasets from Gyoneva et al., 2019 and Connor-Robson et al., 2019; and two proteomics datasets from Connor-Robson et al., 2019. Users can walk through multiple sub-tabs to visualize, select and download figures or data. 2.1 Upload Files The “Upload Files” tab allows users to upload their own data to Quickomics as csv (Comma Separated Values) files. Two kinds of uploads are supported: a complete data set, with a sample metadata file, a normalized expression data file and a statistical comparison results file, or a comparison data file only. Example csv files for RNA-Seq (200 genes from the mouse microglia dataset) and proteomics (200 proteins from the AD/PD dataset) can be downloaded from the links at the top of the tab. To upload, enter a project name, select the species (human, mouse or rat) and choose the files. Detailed formatting guidance is outlined below, Sample Metadata File: It should have “sampleid” and “group” columns, with additional columns optional. Sample identifiers must match those used in the expression data file. This file is not needed for a comparison-only upload. Expression Data File: It should be a matrix of expression values with genes/proteins as rows, and samples as columns. The unique IDs for genes/proteins are in the first column. We recommend using log of normalized expression values, e.g. log2(TPM+1) for RNAseq data or normalized intensity or ratio for proteomics data. The file can be compressed as .gz or .zip. This file is not needed for a comparison-only upload. Comparison Data File: It should have five columns, “UniqueID”, “test”, “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. The comparison names are listed in “test” column. Please note that wrongly named column headers will cause issues. The file can be a csv or txt file, and can be compressed as .gz or .zip. Gene/Protein Name File: By default, Quickomics creates this file from the unique IDs in the data files, so most users don’t need to prepare it; select the type of the unique IDs, which can be Ensembl Gene ID, Gene Symbol, NCBI GeneID, UniProtKB Protein ID or UniProt Protein Name. To upload your own file instead, uncheck “Create Gene/Protein Name File automatically”. It must have four columns: “id” (sequential numbers like 1,2,3 … …), “UniqueID” (matching IDs used in the expression and comparison data file), “Gene.Name” (official gene symbols), “Protein.ID” (UniProt protein IDs, or keep it empty for RNA-Seq data). Additional columns (e.g. gene biotype) are optional. Then click “Submit Data”. After the data files are processed, Quickomics will automatically load all required data for exploration immediately and show a direct URL for the dataset, so that users can come back to it in the future. Behind the scene, gene IDs (Ensembl gene, NCBI gene ID, etc.) are converted into gene symbols by querying the Ensembl BioMart service. If BioMart cannot be reached, a built-in Ensembl annotation table is used instead, or g:Profiler as a last resort, and a note is shown when a backup is used. For protein IDs, we generated a custom lookup table using information downloaded from UniProt Knowledgebase to convert UniProt IDs to gene symbols and protein names. We didn’t use BioMart for proteins as Ensembl databases only cover about 60-80% protein IDs in a typical proteomics data set. 2.2 Prepare R Data Files by Computational Biologists We recommend uploading csv files, which is convenient for general users who can skip section 2.2 entirely. Nevertheless, experienced R programmers can create R data files to be uploaded through “Upload RData File” option. Section 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 provide example R scripts to prepare such R data files for RNA-Seq and proteomics data, respectively. Two R data files are required for each data set, one contains the main data and the other contains gene co-expression network information. For the pre-loaded datasets, main data files are located in the “data” folder, https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/data, and gene co-expression network files are located in the “networkdata” folder, https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/networkdata. One can review the content of a R data file (e.g. Mouse_microglia_RNA-Seq.RData) in the “data” folder by loading it into R. The main R data file contains the following R data frame objects. MetaData: It must have “sampleid”, “group”, “Order” and “ComparePairs” columns. Additional metadata columns about samples are optional. “sampleid” should match those used in expression data. “group” holds group names of samples. “Order” is ordered group names used on plotting. “ComparePairs” are names of comparisons performed. ProteinGeneName: It must have “UniqueID”, “Gene.Name” and “Protein.ID” columns. “UniqueID” matches gene ID in below data_wide and data_long objects. “Gene.Name” should be official gene symbols. “Protein.ID” is UniProt protein IDs, or empty for RNA-Seq data. Additional columns about proteins or genes are optional. data_wide: This is the expression matrix in which rows are genes and columns are samples. Samples must match “sampleid” values in MetaData and gene IDs must match “UniqueID” values in ProteinGeneName. data_long: Gene expression matrix in long format with four columns, “UniqueID”, “sampleid”, “expr” and “group”. “group” values must match those listed in MetaData. results_long: The comparison results in long format with five columns, “UniqueID”, “test”, “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. “UniqueID” matches “UniqueID” in ProteinGeneName. “test” column has the comparison names that must match “ComparePairs” values in MetaData. The other values are typically computed from statistical analysis, but the data headers must be changed to “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. data_results: This is a summary table starting with “UniqueID” and “Gene.Name” columns, then the intensity (max or mean expression value from data_wide for each gene), mean and SD expression values for each group, and finally comparison data (comparison name added as prefix of columns). The network data object is computed from “data_wide” expression matrix by using Hmisc R package exemplified by the code snippet below. cor_res <- Hmisc::rcorr(as.matrix(t(data_wide))) cormat <- cor_res$r pmat <- cor_res$P ut <- upper.tri(cormat) network <- tibble::tibble ( from = rownames(cormat)[row(cormat)[ut]], to = rownames(cormat)[col(cormat)[ut]], cor = signif(cormat[ut], 2), p = signif(pmat[ut], 2), direction = as.integer(sign(cormat[ut])) ) 2.2.1 Example R script to prepare R data files from RNA-Seq results We have provided example input files (TPM and count matrix files, sample grouping file, comparison list file) and the R scripts to generate the main data and network R data files at https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/demo_files/Example_RNA_Seq_data. Please note that you may need to modify RNA_Seq_raw2quickomics.R to fit your input files. • rsem_TPM.txt: The TPM matrix. One can also use RPKM matrix if needed. • rsem_expected_count.txt: The gene count matrix. We used RSEM counts in this case, but gene count results from other methods can be used as well. • grpID.txt: This file lists the group information for each sample. • comparison.txt: This list lists the comparisons to perform (group 1 vs group 2 in each row). The following command will read the above data files, run differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2, and create main and network R data files. $ Rscript RNA_Seq_raw2quickomics.R 2.2.2 Example R script to prepare R data files from proteomics results We have provided the example input files (normalized protein expression, comparison data, sample information, protein and gene names) and the R script to generate the main data and network R data files at https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/demo_files/Example_Proteomics_data. Please note that you may need to modify Proteomics2Quickomics.R to fit your input files. • NormalizedExpression.csv: Normalized protein expression (log2 transformed). • ComparisonData.csv: Comparison results. The statistic values are: logFC, P.Value and Adj.P.Value. This can be created using R packages like limma. • Sample.csv: Sample information file. • ProteinID_Symbol.csv: This file lists the proteinIDs and associate gene symbols. The following command will read the above data files and create main and network R data files. $ Rscript Proteomics2Quickomics.R 2.3 Sample Table A sample table with metadata/details appears upon completion of dataset loading. Here we have selected the “Mouse Microglia RNA” dataset from the previously published paper (Gyoneva et al., 2019) as an example to illustrate all the functionalities. This publication used RNAseq to conclude that the knockout of the Cx3cr1 gene altered the microglial transcriptome in a manner similar to what ageing does, albeit in a milder extent. Using Quickomics, we can visualize the original results from the paper, as well as provide novel visualizations to support new results. The Sample Table contains detailed info of all study samples. A total of 93 samples that were sequenced in this project are listed in the table with attributes like sampleid, group, Age, Genotype and Gender, shown in different columns. 2.4 Project Overview This tab gives an overview of all samples in the project by providing a summary from the metadata. This includes information like which species was used, the different comparisons run and total number of samples in each group. This tab also helps identify how many groups were present in the dataset, like in this project there are 9 different groups that correspond to three genotypes in each of three time points (WT, Het, KO; 2mo, 1yr, 2yr). 2.5 Result Table This tab contains statistical analysis results like Ensemble ID (for RNAseq data) and Accession ID (for proteomics data), gene name, mRNA or protein abundance (count or intensity), mean and SD values for each group, log2 fold change, P value and adjusted P value. 2.6 Data Table The Data table contains normalized expression values (TPM for RNAseq, intensity for label free proteomic quantification, or ratio for isobaric label proteomics quantification) per sample for each gene. This table has a “Download Page” button to download the rows on the current page; to keep the whole table, use “Save to output” (see Chapter 15). 2.7 Protein Gene Names This tab contains all quantified gene or protein IDs and gene names. 2.8 Help Finally, the “Help” feature summarizes what data is being displayed in each tab under Select Dataset. The Help tab is available for all sections of the subsequent analysis.

Chapter 3 Groups and Samples Module The “Groups and Samples” module controls which groups, samples and comparisons are used in most other modules of Quickomics. It was first introduced in version 2.0 and has been redesigned in the current version. Users can keep or remove samples by any sample attribute (for example group, Age, Genotype or Gender), remove individual samples or comparisons, and re-order groups and samples, all by clicking and dragging buttons in an interactive manner. Changes are made in this tab first, and are passed on to the other modules only after the User clicks “Apply Changes to Project Data”. The selection is used by QC Plots, Expression Plot, Heatmap, DEGs, Correlation Analysis, Pattern Clustering, Time Course Analysis and Correlation Network, and by WGCNA when it is run again. Dataset, Gene Set Enrichment and Venn Diagram always use all samples and comparisons of the project, as do the pre-computed WGCNA results. 3.1 Overview of the Groups and Samples tab The tab is organized from top to bottom as shown below, using the Mouse Microglia RNA dataset (Gyoneva et al., 2019) as an example. At the top, “Reset All” restores the original selection of the project, and “Apply Changes to Project Data” passes the current selection on to the other modules. The note next to these buttons shows whether the current selection has been applied. The tip below them is a reminder that several buttons can be picked at once with Ctrl + click (Cmd + click on Mac). Next, each categorical sample attribute has its own row. The values that are kept are listed under “Keep (Drag to Order)” and can be dragged to change their order, while values dragged into the “Remove” box on the right are left out. Attributes that are numeric, have only one value, or have a different value for every sample are not shown as rows. In this dataset, the four rows are group, Age, Genotype and Gender. Below the attribute rows, “Available Samples” lists every sample currently included, and “Available Comparisons” lists the comparisons currently included. Individual samples or comparisons can be dragged into the “Drag to Remove Samples” or “Drag to Remove Comparisons” boxes. The line at the bottom summarizes the current selection, here 93 / 93 samples and 9 / 9 comparisons. 3.2 Remove groups by sample attributes To remove all samples sharing an attribute value, drag that value from “Keep” to the “Remove” box of the same row. In the example below, we drag 2yr from the Age row to “Remove” to focus on the 2mo and 1yr microglia. Quickomics updates everything else automatically: the 2yr_Het, 2yr_KO and 2yr_WT groups are moved to “Remove” in the group row, the 2yr samples are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”, and the four comparisons involving 2yr groups are moved to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”. The summary now shows 64 / 93 samples and 5 / 9 comparisons. The selection is made step by step, so each change starts from the samples currently kept. Dragging a value back to “Keep” adds its samples back, except samples carrying a value that is still removed in another row. The red note “Changes not applied yet. Other tabs still use the previous selection.” is a reminder that the new selection has not been passed on to the other tabs yet (see Section 3.6). 3.3 Select and remove multiple samples Individual samples, for example outliers identified in the QC Plots module, can be removed by dragging them from “Available Samples” to “Drag to Remove Samples”. To move several samples at once, hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) and click each sample; the selected samples are outlined in red. Then drag any one of the selected samples, and all of them move together. Here, the three samples 1yr-Het-11M, 1yr-Het-12M and 1yr-Het-14M are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”. Comparisons that relied on the removed samples are removed as well; in this example 1yr_Hetvs1yr_WT is moved to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”, and the summary shows 61 / 93 samples and 4 / 9 comparisons. Multiple selection works the same way for attribute values and comparisons. 3.4 Remove samples by comparisons Samples can also be selected through the comparisons. When a comparison is dragged from “Available Comparisons” to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”, its samples are removed as well, but only the samples that no remaining comparison uses. In the example below, we remove 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT. The eleven 2yr_KO samples are used only by this comparison, so they are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”, and the 2yr_KO group is moved to “Remove” in the group row. The 2yr_WT samples are kept, because they are still used by 2yr_Hetvs2yr_WT, 2yr_WTvs1yr_WT and 2yr_WTvs2mo_WT. The summary now shows 82 / 93 samples and 8 / 9 comparisons. Dragging a comparison back to “Available Comparisons” adds its samples back. 3.5 Reorder groups and samples The order of the buttons in each “Keep” box sets the order used in plots and tables. In this example, we drag 2mo in front of 1yr in the Age row, so that the younger animals come first. The groups are re-ordered to 2mo_Het, 2mo_KO, 2mo_WT, 1yr_Het, 1yr_KO, 1yr_WT, and the samples in “Available Samples” follow the new order. Groups, samples and comparisons can also be re-ordered directly by dragging them within their own boxes. Re-ordering comparisons does not change which samples are kept. 3.6 Apply changes to all modules When the selection is final, click “Apply Changes to Project Data”. The note changes to “All changes applied.”, and the modules listed at the top of this chapter now use the selected groups, samples and comparisons in the selected order.

Chapter 4 QC Plots Module The “QC Plots” module performs basic QC analyses, as described in following paragraphs, on an uploaded dataset to evaluate integrity and quality of the data. The plots were generated using the ggplot2, ggpubr, plotly, rgl, ComplexHeatmap and factoextra R packages. All QC plots use the groups and samples selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3), and the current selection is shown at the top of the left panel. The width of the left panel can be adjusted with the “Set the Side Menu Width” slider in the upper right corner of the page (15–50% of the page width; the small icon next to it shows or hides the slider). This setting applies to all modules. 4.1 PCA Plot The principle component analysis (PCA) plot displays, by default, the first 2 PC’s in the dataset and colors study groups with “none” selected in shape and size settings. This plot is highly customizable. Users can change the display by annotating the plot with different colors, shapes, size scheme, as well as label selected subsets data points. Any two of the first ten principal components can be selected for the plot. The “Color By” setting is shared with the “PCA 3D Plot”, “PCA 3D Interactive” and “Distance Heatmap” tabs, and “Shape By” is shared with “PCA 3D Interactive”; the other settings apply only to the PCA plot. To illustrate the strengths of customization, we changed a few display elements as shown below, to visualize the influence of Age and Genotype on sample clustering: We added the Plot/Refresh button to graphs that take time to generate. We also enhanced user interface to show plot progress and display initial plot. In the resulting PCA plot, the 2mo groups separate from the 1yr and 2yr groups, mostly along PC2, which agrees with Age being the factor that drives the biggest separation in this dataset. There is some separation driven by the Genotype as well. Two 2mo_KO samples (2mo-KO-7F and 2mo-KO-8F) lie far from all other samples along PC1. The Ellipsoid feature helps group samples by the color attribute, while the Marginal Rug feature helps understand the sample distribution along the axis. Furthermore, the plot can be saved in high resolution by clicking on “Save to Output”. Chapter 15 of this document describes the next steps of downloading and obtaining the saved plots. 4.2 Covariates The Covariates tab provides flexibility to visualize the covariates, such as Age, group, Genotype showing here. This table contains several columns including the Significance, p-value, and FDR for each covariates listed. Users can also adjust the covariates and cutoffs on the left. 4.3 AlignQC The AlignQC tab contains several sub-tabs to visualize the QC metrics of the alignment step. Here, we can check the ‘Top Gene Ratio’, ‘Top Gene List’, ‘Mapped Read Allocation’, or ‘Plot Other Variables’ across samples. More details can be adjusted on the left panel, such as the height, width, and font size of the plot. The ‘Save to output’ function can add the current plot in the output list. The “Mapped Read Allocation” sub-tab needs the columns Exonic_Rate, Intronic_Rate and Intergenic_Rate in the sample table, and “Plot Other Variables” needs at least one numeric column, such as RIN or read counts. 4.4 Eigenvalues By default, the PCA plot displays PC1 and PC2 as described in Section 4.1. However, in many cases other PC’s may be important in explaining additional variance in the dataset. This sub-tab generates a plot of the variances versus the first 10 PCs in the dataset, with bars for the percentage of variance explained by each PC and a red line for the cumulative variance, enabling Users to make educated decisions of which PCs to plot in 2D scatter plot. In this dataset PC1 and PC2 together explain around 27% of the variance. PC2 and PC3 were used to redo the PCA plot, but here the factors driving the separation of the samples is not as clear. 4.5 PCA 3D Plot This sub-tab contains a way to perform 3D PCA representation. The functionality is limited to doing so only on PC1, PC2 and PC3. Users can zoom in and out to focus on different areas of the plot or rotate the plot in different axes to find the best separation by age as shown below. There are 3 attributes that can be changed: color, ellipsoid inclusion, and labels of the samples. The “Color By” and “Plot Ellipsoid” attributes were changed in the following plot. This highlights the clear separation of samples by Age and not Genotype, contrary to the original biological hypothesis. 4.6 PCA 3D Interactive This tab is similar to the previous one (4.5 PCA 3D Plot), but here users have the additional capability to hover over the samples on the plot to identify more details, see the pointer below. This was implemented through the plotly package in R. Users can change 2 attributes here, the color and shape. In the plot below, the “Color By” and “Shape By” attributes have been changed to highlight the drivers of separation. 4.7 Sample-sample Distance This tab helps identify pair-wise similarity between all samples. It has three sub-tabs: “Distance Heatmap”, “Correlation Heatmap” and “Correlation Data Table”. A short description above each heatmap explains how it is computed. Here again, Users have the option to save the heatmaps to output. The “Distance Heatmap” shows the Euclidean distance between every sample pair, computed from the expression values. Smaller distances mean that two samples have more similar overall expression profiles. By default, the rows and columns are clustered based on similarity; this can be turned off with “Apply Clustering”. The annotation bar shows the samples colored by the “Color By” attribute, which is shared with the PCA plots, and “Show More Options” gives control over the font sizes and the plot height. It is clear from this plot that samples of the same Age have the smaller distances, that is, they have closer gene expression patterns. The “Correlation Heatmap” shows the correlation between every sample pair. Unlike the distance, the correlation is scale-invariant, so it highlights shared expression patterns rather than absolute differences in expression. Users can choose how the samples are annotated (“Annotate By”) and labeled (“Axis Label By”), and whether to apply clustering. Selecting “Yes” under “Show More Options” gives further control over the heatmap colors, the colors of the annotations (set automatically by a random seed, selected from palettes, or uploaded as a csv file), font sizes and plot height. In this example, the samples are annotated by Age, and samples of the same Age are highly correlated with each other. The “Correlation Data Table” lists the correlation values of all sample pairs in a searchable table, which can be downloaded by page or as a whole. 4.8 Dendrograms Like the previous plot (4.7 Sample-sample Distance), the Dendrogram plot helps visualize hierarchical clustering relationships between samples. The Default plot is Circular and cut into four parts. Users have the option to visualize in two other ways (tree or horizontal) and cut the plot in multiple regions. Here again, Users can save the plot to output. In the plot below, we have selected to visualize as a tree and cut into eight parts. This shows the relationship between the samples to help understand the hierarchal clustering. Overall, the samples are arranged by age, but there are some outliers that appear. The 2mo samples form their own branches, while the 2yr samples cluster together with part of the 1yr samples. 4.9 Box Plot The Boxplot is a visualization to understand the distribution of the normalized expression levels in all samples. To keep the plot fast, it uses up to 2,000 randomly picked genes/proteins per sample. This identifies the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum values in the dataset. In this demo dataset, most of the samples have the same range of expression, indicating that there are no outliers. 4.10 CV Distribution This plot shows the histogram of CVs (coefficient of variation) and a dashed line for each group indicates the median CV, labeled with its value and the group name. In this dataset, the 2mo_KO samples have the highest CV while the 2yr_Het samples have the lowest variability, which corresponds to what is visually seen on the PCA plot for these samples in Section 4.1. 4.11 Help The Help section describes each tab of the QC Plot and what is being visualized. For further help please visit the GitHub containing the source code for this tools (https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics) or click on the link at the bottom of the page.

Chapter 5 Expression Plot Module This functional module allows Users to browse through a subset of genes/proteins. It also offers an option to plot expression of individually selected genes. Four different displays: Box Plot, Bar Plot, Violin Plot and Line Plot are made available to fit the Users’ preference. 5.1 Browsing This tab lets the Users plot out the expression of the DEGs/DEPs identified in the different comparisons. Chapter 8 Gene Set Enrichment Module 8.1 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) 8.2 Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) 8.3 Gene Expression 8.4 Gene Set Heat Map 8.5 KEGG Pathway View 8.6 WikiPathways View 8.7 Dot Plot

Chapter 8 Gene Set Enrichment Module This functionality in Quickomics is an extension to the differential gene identification. Users are able to use different cutoffs to filter out DEGs/DEPs in different comparisons and probe enriched pathways. This is a useful way to make biological sense of the data. In the current version, the module offers two enrichment methods, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA, Section 8.1) and Over-Representation Analysis (ORA, Section 8.2), and several views of the results: Gene Expression (8.3), Gene Set Heatmap (8.4), KEGG Pathway View (8.5), WikiPathways View (8.6) and Dot Plot (8.7). The two major updates of this module in the current version are multi-comparison support and the Dot Plot. GSEA and ORA can now be run for several comparisons at once by selecting them under “Select 1 or More Comparisons for Analysis” (or checking “Select All Comparisons”), and the KEGG Pathway View can show the fold changes of several comparisons in the same pathway diagram. The new Dot Plot (Section 8.7) then summarizes the GSEA or ORA results of these comparisons in one figure, so that the enriched gene sets can be compared across comparisons at a glance. This module always uses all samples and comparisons of the project, not the selection made in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3). 8.1 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) The “Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)” tab tests whether the genes of a gene set change together in a comparison. Select the comparison(s), the ranking method, the gene set size range, the adjusted P-value cutoff and the gene set collections, then click “Compute/Refresh”. By default, gene sets with 15 to 1,000 genes are tested and those with an adjusted P value below 0.25 are listed; checking “Collapse Gene Sets” keeps only the independent gene sets and leaves out those that mostly overlap with a more significant one. In the results table, a positive normalized enrichment score (NES) means that the gene set is up-regulated, and a negative NES means that it is down-regulated. The “Copy Leading Edge Genes” button copies the genes that drive the enrichment, so that they can be pasted into other modules. Clicking a gene set name in the GSEA or ORA results table selects it for the Gene Expression, Gene Set Heatmap, KEGG Pathway View and WikiPathways View tabs. To demonstrate usage of this functionality, we will use the Mouse Microglia RNA dataset to help answer the question which pathways were altered by Genotype and/or Age. Very similar to the results from Gyoneva et al., 2019, this analysis points to immune related terms being down-regulated in 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT. In the example below for 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, complement and coagulation cascades and viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor have negative NES values; the same pathways are also found by ORA in the down-regulated genes (Section 8.2). 8.2 Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) The “Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)” tab tests whether the DEGs/DEPs of a comparison are over-represented in gene sets. Unlike GSEA (Section 8.1), which ranks all genes of a comparison by logFC or by -log(P-Value) and tests whether the genes of a gene set are found at the top or bottom of the ranked list, ORA uses only the genes passing the cutoffs. Users pick one or more comparisons, apply cutoff criteria, choose up-, down- or both-regulated genes, and select the gene set collections; then click “Compute/Refresh” to run the analysis. Gene sets with an adjusted P value below 0.05 (“ORA p.adj Cutoff”) are listed, and “Collapse Gene Sets” works as in GSEA. Instead of the DEGs/DEPs of a comparison, “Genes Used for ORA” can also be set to “Gene List” to test a pasted list of genes, against either the genes in the current project or the genes in the gene sets as background (“Background Genes”); in this case the Gene Expression, Gene Set Heatmap and KEGG Pathway View tabs are not available. Gene sets are available for human, mouse and rat. “Gene Set Species” is set to the species of the project when it is human, mouse or rat. When the gene sets come from another species than the project, “Gene Symbol Mapping” converts the gene symbols; it is set to “Homologous Genes” automatically, and the symbols can also be changed to upper case (human) or title case (mouse/rat), or used as they are. These settings, as well as “Add Custom GeneSet”, which adds gene sets entered in a text box or uploaded as a GMT file, apply to both GSEA and ORA. In the example below, we used the same comparison, 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, with human KEGG pathways with homologous gene mapping, a Fold Change Cutoff of 1.43 and a P value cutoff of 0.01; the top down-regulated pathways include cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, complement and coagulation cascades, and hematopoietic cell lineage. Similarly, we select the up-regulated genes. Four KEGG pathways are enriched: rheumatoid arthritis, antigen processing and presentation, fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, and leishmaniasis. 8.3 Gene Expression For the enriched terms identified in the GSEA (Section 8.1) or ORA (Section 8.2) tab, Users have the ability to look at the differential values of the genes present in the set. Click a gene set name in the ORA or GSEA results table, then open the “Gene Expression” tab. It shows the statistics of the gene set and lists all genes in the set with their logFC, P value and adjusted P value; the DE genes used in the ORA, or the leading-edge genes of a GSEA gene set, are shown in green. Here we are probing hsa04061 Viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, identified in the down-regulated category; 7 of its 42 genes, such as CX3CR1, CCR2 and CCR5, are down-regulated DE genes. 8.4 Gene Set Heat Map Like the “Gene Expression” tab, Users have the ability to plot expression of the genes in the pathway term selected as a heatmap. For each gene in the set, the heatmap shows the mean expression of the samples in each group (the “group” attribute), scaled per gene (z-score). “From the Gene Set, Show” chooses between all genes of the set and only the DE genes (ORA) or leading-edge genes (GSEA). This visualization shows that while the genes of the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway are enriched in the down-regulated genes, not all of them change in the same direction across the groups. 8.5 KEGG Pathway View This functionality is available only to KEGG pathway terms. Users have the option to view the Fold Change levels of different genes in the KEGG pathway selected for one or more comparisons. In this example we demo the KEGG pathway “hsa04612 Antigen processing and presentation” for the 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT and 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT comparisons. Each gene box shows one color per comparison. “Gene log2FC Range” and “Compound log2FC Range” set the log2 fold change that gets the full color, and “Map Symbols to KEGG Nodes?” labels the gene boxes with the gene symbols. This figure identifies all the genes that are differentially expressed in this pathway. Most genes in the MHC I pathway change little, while CD74 in the MHC II pathway is down-regulated in both comparisons. The visualization is also useful to highlight whether or not a large proportion of genes in a pathway are altered by the perturbation. 8.6 WikiPathways View This tab shows the logFC values of the selected comparison on a WikiPathways diagram. Select a pathway by clicking its name in the ORA or GSEA results table, or choose it from the “Wikipathways for Visualization” list. The colors for low, middle and high logFC values and the log2FC range can be changed in the left panel. In the example below, we show the Microglia pathogen phagocytosis pathway (WP3937) for 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT; up-regulated genes are shown in red and down-regulated genes in green. 8.7 Dot Plot The Dot Plot compares the enrichment results of several comparisons in one figure. First run GSEA or ORA for the comparisons of interest and choose the same “Analysis Type” in the left panel. The comparisons to plot can be re-ordered or removed by dragging them. The table above the plot lists how many of the plotted gene sets come from each comparison. The dot size shows -log10 of the adjusted P value, and the dot color shows the NES for GSEA results or the number of DE genes in the gene set for ORA results. Chapter 9 WGCNA Module Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) finds groups of genes, called modules, whose expression goes up and down together across the samples. Genes in the same module often work in the same biological process. Each module is summarized by its eigengene, a single profile that represents the expression of all genes of the module, and the eigengenes can be correlated with sample attributes such as Age or Genotype to find the modules linked to them. WGCNA takes a long time to compute, so Quickomics loads pre-computed results when a project has them. For the Mouse Microglia demo dataset, the results were pre-computed with the 10,000 most variable genes and a Dendrogram Cut Height for Merging of 0.25, and they are shown as soon as the WGCNA tab is opened. Users can change the number of genes or the cut height in the left panel and click “Run” to compute new results; this can take 3–10 minutes. The pre-computed results use all samples of the project, while “Run” uses the samples selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3). When the selected samples are the same as those of the pre-computed results and the number of genes is unchanged or within 10%, for example when only the cut height is changed, “Run” reuses the saved pre-computed data and finishes faster. Otherwise, everything is computed again from the start, including the soft-thresholding power, and the process takes several minutes. The tabs are described below in the order of a typical analysis: WGCNA QC (Section 9.1), WGCNA Result (9.2), Module Eigengenes (9.3) and Module-Trait Relationships (9.4). In the app, WGCNA QC is the fourth tab, after Module-Trait Relationships. Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide, and the “Help” tab describes the whole workflow. 9.1 WGCNA QC Before the network is built, WGCNA raises the correlations between genes to a power, called the soft-thresholding power. A higher power keeps the strong correlations and pushes the weak ones toward zero. The “Soft-Thresholding Power” sub-tab shows how well the network fits a scale-free topology (SFT.R.sq) and the mean connectivity of the genes for each power. The usual choice is the lowest power with an R² above 0.8, which is marked by the red line in the Scale Independence plot. For the demo dataset, power 6 is the first power above this line, with an R² of 0.906 and a mean connectivity of 301, and it is highlighted in the table as the power used. The “WGCNA Network” sub-tab helps check the data before the network is built. The histogram shows the distribution of the gene variance across the samples; WGCNA uses only the most variable genes, set by “Select Top N Genes”, to reduce noise and computing time. The dendrogram below clusters the samples by their overall expression profiles. Samples of the same group are expected to cluster together, and a sample that joins the others only at a much greater height may be an outlier; such a sample can be removed in the “Groups and Samples” module before clicking “Run” again. In the demo dataset, the samples cluster mainly by age, and the sample 2yr-WT-2F joins the others at the greatest height. 9.2 WGCNA Result The “Dendrogram Plot” sub-tab shows how the genes are clustered by their co-expression. The colored bar below the tree shows the module of each gene: genes of the same module share a color, and grey genes are not assigned to any module. Modules whose eigengenes are very similar are merged; a lower “Dendrogram Cut Height for Merging” keeps more, smaller modules. The “Gene Cluster Summary Table” sub-tab lists each module with its number of genes and the genes it contains. In the demo dataset there are six modules plus 4,238 grey genes, with sizes from 79 genes in the red module to 2,569 genes in the turquoise module. For each module, “Copy all genes” copies its genes so that they can be pasted into other modules of Quickomics, and “Run ORA” runs Over-Representation Analysis on its genes (see Section 8.2). For example, the yellow module includes Xist and Tsix. “Save GCT data file to output” saves the expression data with the module of each gene, which can be downloaded from the Output module (Chapter 15). 9.3 Module Eigengenes The “Eigengene table” sub-tab lists the eigengene value of every module in every sample. Each row is one sample and each column is one module. In the example below, the blue module (ME5_blue) has positive values in the 2mo samples, which matches its high correlation with Age2mo in Section 9.4. The table can be saved with “Save to output”. The “Eigengene Network” sub-tab shows how the modules relate to each other. In the tree at the top, modules with similar eigengenes are joined at a lower height; in the heatmap below, red means that two eigengenes are similar and blue means they are not. In the demo dataset, the blue and brown modules are joined first, and the red module is close to them. 9.4 Module-Trait Relationships The “Module Trait Heatmap” sub-tab correlates the eigengene of each module with the sample attributes. Select the attributes, choose a base level for each, and click “Plot Module Trait Correlation”. Each level of an attribute becomes one column of the heatmap; red cells mean that the genes of the module are, on average, more highly expressed in the samples of that level than in the other samples, and blue cells mean that they are less expressed. Hovering over a cell shows the correlation and its P value, and clicking a cell opens the “Hub Gene Identification Table” sub-tab with the trait and the module of that cell already selected. In the example below, we selected Age, Genotype and Gender. The blue module has the strongest correlation, 0.94 with Age2mo, so its genes are higher in the 2mo samples. The green module shows the opposite pattern, with a correlation of −0.87 with Age2mo and 0.79 with Age2yr. As in the earlier chapters, Age has a much larger effect than Genotype, and the yellow module, which includes Xist and Tsix, is correlated with GenderF. Hub genes are the most connected genes of a module and are often key genes of the process it represents. In the “Hub Gene Identification Table” sub-tab, select a trait and optionally a module, then click “Run”; when the sub-tab is opened by clicking a cell of the heatmap, the trait and module are already filled in, and only “Run” needs to be clicked. For each gene, the table lists its connectivity within the module, its module membership (the correlation of the gene with the module eigengene) and its gene significance (the correlation of the gene with the trait), with their P values. In the example below, we clicked the cell of the blue module and Age2mo in the heatmap above, so the trait Age2mo and the module ME5_blue were filled in, and then clicked “Run”. The 895 genes are sorted by connectivity, and the top hub genes include several histone genes, such as Hist1h2ac, Hist4h4 and Hist1h3e. The “Hub Gene Identification Plot” sub-tab shows the same results as two plots. Both plots are made by the same “Run” as the table, for the same trait and module, and each dot is one of the 895 genes in the table; hovering over a dot shows its row of the table. In the example below, the dot at the top right of the right plot is Hist1h2ac, the first gene of the table. The left plot compares the module membership and the gene significance of each gene; in the blue module they are highly correlated (cor = 0.968), which means that the genes most central to the module are also the most related to Age2mo. The right plot shows the connectivity of each gene against its module membership, and the top 10% most connected genes, the hub genes, are shown in red; they are the genes at the top of the table.

Chapter 10 Correlation Analysis Module 10.1 Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group 10.2 Gene-Target

Chapter 10 Correlation Analysis Module This module measures how closely two things change together across the samples. Four types of correlation are offered under “Correlation Type”. Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group correlate each pair of the selected genes, samples or groups (Section 10.1). Gene-Target correlates every gene with one target, which can be a gene or a sample attribute such as Age (Section 10.2). To see the correlation of all samples at once, use the sample correlation heatmap in the QC Plots module (Chapter 4). This module uses the samples selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3). Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide. 10.1 Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group Select the correlation type and the genes, samples or groups to compare, choose Pearson for linear relationships or Spearman for relationships that go in one direction but need not be linear, and click “Compute/Refresh”. Genes can be selected by name, browsed (“Browsing” takes the DEGs/DEPs of one of the selected comparisons that pass the fold change and P value or adjusted P value cutoffs, all of them or only the up- or down-regulated ones), entered as a list with “Upload Genes”, or taken from a gene set. The “Result Table” lists every pair with its correlation, R squared and P value, ranked from the strongest correlation. In the example below, we entered the MHC class II genes H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, H2-Eb1 and Cd74 together with Cx3cr1. The MHC class II genes are highly correlated with each other, with correlations from 0.91 to 0.98, while their correlations with Cx3cr1 are lower, between 0.55 and 0.66. Clicking “View Correlation Plot” in a row opens the “Correlation Plot” tab with the scatter plot of that pair. Each dot is a sample, and the plot shows the correlation, the regression line and its equation, and the P value. Below is the plot for H2-Aa and H2-Ab1, with a correlation of 0.980. The “Data Table” tab lists the values used. Sample-Sample and Group-Group correlations are set up in the same way, by selecting at least two samples, or an attribute and at least two of its groups. These correlations are computed over the genes chosen under “Genes Used in Correlation Analysis”: all genes (the default), or the genes from Browsing, Upload Genes or a gene set. Group-Group correlations use the mean expression of each group. 10.2 Gene-Target Gene-Target correlates every gene with one target across the individual samples, to find the genes that go up and down with it. The target can be a gene or a sample attribute. Numeric attributes, such as a dose or a score, are used as they are. For text levels with an order, choose “Ordered levels” and list the levels from lowest to highest; Spearman correlation is then used. Because the ages of the demo dataset are given in different units (2mo, 1yr and 2yr), the app uses “Ordered levels” for Age, and we put the levels in the order 2mo, 1yr, 2yr. After clicking “Compute/Refresh”, the table lists all 15,402 genes sorted by their correlation with Age. Crlf2, St14, Mageh1 and H2-Q6 have the highest correlations, above 0.93, while genes such as Gm10616 and Ctf2 have negative correlations, so they decrease with age. The samples can also be limited to some levels of an attribute with “Restrict samples to”. The table can be saved with “Save table to output”. Clicking a row in the table shows the gene in the “Gene-Target Plot” tab. Each dot is a sample, and the line shows the trend. Crlf2 increases steadily from 2mo to 1yr to 2yr, with a Spearman correlation of 0.94. With “Compute separately for each level of”, the correlation is computed separately within each level of another attribute, and the table gets one set of columns per level. In the example below, we computed the correlation with Age separately for each genotype. For each genotype, Het, KO and WT, the table gives the correlation of each gene with Age (r), its P value, adjusted P value and number of samples (n). max_abs_r is the largest absolute correlation of the three, and the table is sorted by it. For example, the top gene, Rxrg, has correlations of 0.921 in Het, 0.943 in KO and 0.892 in WT. The “Correlation Heatmap” tab then shows the correlations of the top genes in the table, one column per level, with red for positive and blue for negative correlations; the number of genes is set with “Top genes to show”. The heatmap follows the order of the table, so sorting the table by the column of one genotype, such as WT_r, shows the top genes of that genotype instead. Below are the 30 genes with the highest max_abs_r. The top 30 genes have the same direction in Het, KO and WT, so their change with age does not depend on the genotype.

Chapter 11 Pattern Clustering Module 11.1 Clustering of Centroid Profiles 11.2 Data Table

Chapter 11 Pattern Clustering Module This functional module in Quickomics helps cluster genes/proteins based on their expression profiles across different groups. Two different algorithms, soft (fuzzy) clustering and k-means, are implemented. The current version adds three major updates. First, the genes can be clustered by any sample attribute, not only by group: “Select Pattern Variable” chooses the attribute, such as Age or Genotype, and each gene is summarized by its mean expression in each level of that attribute. Second, “Cluster On” decides what the clusters are based on: the trend only (z-score, the default), the trend together with the size of the change (centred values), or the mean expression without any transformation. Third, the levels of the attribute can be easily re-ordered or removed by dragging them above the plot, which sets the order of the levels in the plot and leaves the removed levels out of the clustering. The means are computed from the samples selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3); if the pattern differs between conditions, the samples can first be limited to one condition there. 11.1 Clustering of Centroid Profiles Users have the option to either select the DEGs/DEPS as the list of genes/proteins to cluster based off on or upload a custom gene list. DEGs/DEPs can be selected from one of the comparisons selected in “Groups and Samples” or from all of them (“ALL”), and cutoffs can be applied to limit the number of genes. Users also choose the sample attribute to plot, how the expression values are transformed before clustering (“Cluster On”, described in the guide above the plot), and the order of the groups; then click “Plot/Refresh”. “Cluster Method” chooses between the two algorithms, and “Cluster Number” sets the number of clusters (2 to 12, 6 by default). K-means assigns each gene to one cluster and draws the cluster mean as a thick line. Soft clustering (Mfuzz fuzzy c-means) gives each gene a membership between 0 and 1 in every cluster, and draws the genes with a membership of at least 0.4, colored by membership from red (strong member) to yellow (weak member). In this example below, we select the DEGs/DEPs from all comparisons with a Fold Change cutoff of 3 and a P value cutoff of 0.01, which gives 177 genes, and identify 6 clusters of genes. Please note that this visualization for this dataset is novel and was not previously reported in Gyoneva et al., 2019. The genes in each cluster can be viewed in the “Data Table” tab. 11.2 Data Table The data table contains genes from the previous clusters, along with their gene names and the values used for clustering, here the z-scores of the group means; the “cluster” column gives the cluster number shown in the previous tab. The layout of the table is set by “Data Output Format” in the left panel. By default, the table is shown in the wide format: each gene is shown in one row, the values of the groups are in separate columns, from 2mo_WT to 2yr_KO, followed by the cluster number. In the long format, each gene is shown in one row per group. In this example there are nine groups, so each gene appears in nine rows, and the table has 1,593 rows for the 177 genes. Each row gives the group, the gene, the “mean” column with the mean expression of the gene in that group, the “value” column with the z-score used for clustering, and the cluster number. For example, Clec10a has a mean expression of 3.33 in 2mo_WT and 1.38 in 2yr_WT; after the z-score transformation these become 1.69 and -0.391, and the gene belongs to cluster 2, the genes that are high in the 2mo groups and low in the 1yr and 2yr groups. The long format is useful when the table is downloaded to make plots or to filter the data in other software.

Chapter 12 Time Course Analysis Module 12.1 Time-Series DE Analysis 12.2 DEG Clustering Analysis 12.3 Similar Pattern Search

Chapter 12 Time Course Analysis Module This module finds genes whose expression changes over time, groups them by the shape of their time pattern, and finds genes that follow the same pattern as a gene of interest. Any sample attribute with ordered levels can be used as the time variable. The Mouse Microglia demo dataset has no real time series, but its three ages (2mo, 1yr and 2yr) can be used as time points, and Genotype can be used as the condition. The module has three tabs, described below: Time-Series DE Analysis (Section 12.1), DEG Clustering Analysis (12.2) and Similar Pattern Search (12.3). The analysis uses the samples selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3). Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide to its method. 12.1 Time-Series DE Analysis Select the time variable and, optionally, one or more condition variables, then choose the method and the test and click “Run Time-Series DE Analysis”. Two methods are offered: a DESeq2 likelihood ratio test (LRT) for RNA-seq counts and a limma F-test for continuous log values such as proteomics data; the default is chosen from the expression unit of the project. Because the raw read counts are usually not available in Quickomics, the DESeq2 method converts the log expression values (for example log2(TPM+1)) back to the linear scale, using the log base and the small value taken from the expression unit of the project (2 and 1 when the unit does not give them), rounds them to whole numbers and treats these TPM-like values as counts. The results are therefore an approximation of a count-based analysis. For limma, “Min. Non-missing Values per Condition x Time Group” (2 by default) sets how many values each condition and time point needs. Two tests are offered. “Time x Condition” (the default) finds genes whose trend over time is different between the conditions, and “Time only” finds genes that change over time. Unlike the DEG module, the P values describe the whole trend of a gene, not a single fold change between two groups. In the example below, we used Age as the time variable, no condition variable, the DESeq2 method and the Time only test, so the analysis asks which genes change with age in all samples together. Many genes change with age. The genes with the smallest adjusted P values below the cutoff of 0.1 are listed, up to the number set in “Select Number of Top DEGs for Clustering” (1,000 by default, 300 to 1,500); here 989 genes are listed, all with adjusted P values far below 0.1. The max_time_log2FC column gives the log2 fold change between the time points with the highest and the lowest mean expression. The top gene, Zfp36, has the smallest P value and a max_time_log2FC of 2.26. The table can be saved with “Save to output”. 12.2 DEG Clustering Analysis This tab groups the significant genes from Section 12.1 into clusters of genes with the same time pattern. The clusters are found with the degPatterns function of the DEGreport package, which chooses the number of clusters itself. Set the “Minimum Genes per Cluster” (16 by default) and click “Run Clustering”; smaller clusters are left out, so this number may need to be lowered when there are few significant genes. The “Time Series Cluster Plot” sub-tab shows one panel per cluster, with the number of genes in its title. The box plots show the expression of the genes in the cluster at each age, scaled as z-scores, and the line shows the trend; when a condition variable is used, there is one box and one line per condition. Note that the plot gives the ages in years, so 2mo is shown as 0.164yr. In the example below, 980 of the 989 genes fall into three clusters. The 575 genes of cluster 1 are highest at 2mo and decrease with age. The 381 genes of cluster 3 show the opposite pattern and are highest at 2yr. The 24 genes of cluster 2 go up from 2mo to 1yr and drop at 2yr. The “DEG Cluster Result” sub-tab lists the genes of each cluster. “Copy all genes” copies them so they can be pasted into other modules, and “Create Expression Plot” shows their expression in the Expression Plot module (Chapter 5). The “Time-series Sample Heatmap” and “Time-series Group Heatmap” sub-tabs show the genes of the clusters as heatmaps, one column per sample or one column per group. The samples or groups can be annotated with sample attributes (“Annotate Samples” or “Annotate Groups”), the genes can be clustered within each cluster (“Cluster genes”), and “Show More Options” sets the annotation colors, heatmap height and titles. Click “Plot/Refresh” to draw the heatmap after changing the settings. In the group heatmap below, the columns are the three ages, and the rows are the genes, split by cluster. Cluster 1 is red at 2mo and blue at 2yr, and cluster 3 is the reverse. The data behind each heatmap can be saved as a GCT file with the buttons above it. 12.3 Similar Pattern Search This tab finds genes whose expression changes over time in the same way as a chosen gene, or in the opposite way. Run the Time-Series DE Analysis first, then type a gene in “Gene to Match”, choose whether to search only among the significant genes (the default) or among all tested genes, choose “Similar pattern” or “Opposite pattern” and the similarity measure (Kendall, Pearson or Spearman; Pearson by default), and click “Find Similar Genes”. By default, the 50 most similar genes are listed (“Number of Similar Genes to List”) and the top 10 are plotted (“Number of Top Similar Genes to Plot”). “Plot Scale” shows the values as centred log2 values, which keep the size of the changes (the default), or as z-scores. The plot shows the mean expression of the chosen gene, the seed gene, as a red dashed line, together with the most similar genes, for each condition and time point. The table ranks the genes by how well their pattern matches the seed gene (pearson_r with the default Pearson similarity, where 1 is a perfect match); change_distance shows how close the size of the changes is, with smaller values meaning closer to the seed gene, and DE_padj and DE_pvalue give the adjusted and the raw P value of the gene from Section 12.1. A blank DE_padj means that DESeq2 left the gene out of the adjustment because of its low counts; DE_pvalue can then be checked instead. In the example below, we searched the significant genes for genes similar to Zfp36. The top genes, such as Dusp1, Hist2h2aa2, Ier2 and Fos, are also high at 2mo and lower at 1yr and 2yr, with pearson_r close to 1. “Copy seed + selected genes” and “Create Expression Plot” pass the genes to other modules, and the plot and table can be saved to the output.

Chapter 13 Correlation Network Module 13.1 visNetwork 13.2 networkD3 13.3 Data Table

Chapter 13 Correlation Network Module This module helps build co-expression networks based on gene-gene or protein-protein correlations. This is especially useful during co-immunoprecipitation or pulldown proteomics experiments to identify protein partners. Users have the ability to enter 1 or more genes/proteins to identify if their expression is correlated. The network is built from the Pearson correlations between all pairs of genes/proteins across the samples; when a project has more than 10,000 genes/proteins, the 10,000 most variable ones are used. Only pairs with an absolute correlation above 0.7 and a P value below 0.05 are kept (stricter cutoffs are used when there are too many pairs). Pre-computed networks are used when all samples are selected. When samples are removed in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3), the network is computed again for the selected samples, which can take a few minutes. 13.1 visNetwork This uses the R package visNetwork to visualize the expression of correlated genes/proteins. Users have the ability to choose the r and P value cutoffs for selecting the correlated genes/proteins. “Choose r Cutoff” (0.9 by default) is applied to the absolute correlation, so negative correlations are included too, and “Choose P Value Cutoff” offers 0.0001 to 0.05 (0.01 by default). The left panel shows the number of nodes (genes/proteins) and edges (correlated pairs) for the current settings. The “Generate” button, which draws the network, appears when the network has 1 to 200 nodes; otherwise a message asks Users to change the cutoffs or the selected genes. In this example below, we probe 3 genes, Gnai3, Klf6 and Btbd9, with the r cutoff lowered to 0.78, and identify the expression of other genes that are correlated with them. The following network plot was produced. Gnai3 is part of a large network with 66 genes correlated with it. On the other hand, Klf6 was correlated with 2 other genes, Phyhd1 and Tmem189, while Btbd9 was not correlated with any genes at these cutoffs, so it is not shown. 13.2 networkD3 The “networkD3” tab draws the same network with the networkD3 R package, as a force-directed network: the nodes and edges are the same as in the visNetwork tab, and the layout is formed by the nodes pushing each other apart while the edges pull correlated nodes together. Nodes can be dragged with the mouse, and the network can be zoomed in and out. This tab is also drawn when “Generate” is clicked. 13.3 Data Table The edges of the network are listed in this tab. Each row is one pair of correlated genes/proteins, with the correlation (cor), its P value (p) and the direction of the correlation (1 for positive and -1 for negative). “Select Gene Label” shows the genes by gene name or by UniqueID. Users can perform searches and sort based on correlation statistics, and the table can be downloaded by page or as a whole.

Chapter 14 Venn Diagram Module 14.1 Venn Diagram 14.2 Venn Diagram (black & white) 14.3 Intersection Output 14.4 DEG Table

Chapter 14 Venn Diagram Module This module in Quickomics helps Users identify DEGs/DEPs that are common or unique to different comparisons. The DEGs/DEPs are shown as a Venn diagram that can be customized, and as tables that list the genes. The tabs of “Venn Diagram from Current Project” are described below: Venn Diagram (Section 14.1), Venn Diagram (black & white) (14.2), Intersection Output (14.3) and DEG Table (14.4). This module always uses all comparisons of the project, not the selection made in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3). The “Venn Diagram Across Projects” tab works in a similar way with comparisons from different projects. There, each of up to five lists is a data set, chosen from the projects listed on the server, together with one of its comparisons; the tab has its own fold change and P value cutoffs, and “Upper Case Gene Symbols (e.g. mouse vs human)?” converts the gene symbols to upper case so that genes from different species can be matched. 14.1 Venn Diagram To view the DEGs/DEPs as a Venn Diagram, Users have the option to select the fold change and P value cutoffs, whether to use all DEGs/DEPs or only the Up or Down regulated ones, and up to 5 comparisons, each with its own color. In the example below, we used a fold change cutoff of 1.2 and a P value cutoff of 0.01, and selected the three KO vs WT comparisons, 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT and 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT. The panel on the right customizes the diagram, for example its title, the opacity of the colors, the lines and the fonts. Long comparison names can be wrapped onto several lines with “Wrap Labels At (characters)”, or shown as a legend below the diagram. “Save to output” saves the diagram to the Output module (Chapter 15). In this example there were 33 DEGs that were identified in the three comparisons probed here, which represent the set of genes altered by the KO genotype at each of the time points. 14.2 Venn Diagram (black & white) This tab has the same plot seen before in Section 14.1 but highly simplified and in black and white. 14.3 Intersection Output This tab lists the genes in each region of the Venn diagram, one row per region. The “Intersection” column gives the comparisons that share the genes, one name per line; “Count” gives the number of genes, and “Genes” lists them. Long lists show the first 50 genes; click “Show all” to see the rest. “Label name” in the left panel sets whether the genes are shown by gene name, accession number or UniqueID. To copy genes, click one or more rows; the “Copy Selected Gene List” button then copies the genes of all selected rows, without duplicates, so that they can be pasted into other modules. In the example below, we selected the 40 genes found in 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT and 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT and the 33 genes found in all three comparisons, 73 genes together. 14.4 DEG Table This tab lets the Users view the Fold Change and p value of the genes identified in the Venn Diagram in the comparisons being queried. The table includes every gene found in at least one of the selected comparisons, 1,454 genes in this example, with its log fold change, P value and adjusted P value in each comparison. The table can be downloaded with the CSV and Excel buttons, or saved with “Save to output”.

Chapter 15 Output Module 15.1 Download Plots and Tables 15.2 Save Session 15.3 Diagnostics

Chapter 15 Output Module This final tab in Quickomics is used to download the plots, tables and heatmap data saved during the analysis (Section 15.1), to save the settings of a session and restore them later (Section 15.2), and to help troubleshoot problems (Diagnostics, Section 15.3). 15.1 Download Plots and Tables Plots can be downloaded here in high resolution, including for use in publications. Users can save different plots by clicking on “Save to Output” present on the top left corner of the plot during analysis and exploration of the datasets in all previous tabs. Upon clicking on the “Output” tab as seen in the image below, Users can see a list of plots that are available to download to their local machine. The checked plots are downloaded together as one PDF file with “Download PDF”, while “Download SVG” saves only the first selected plot. “Plot File Page Width” and “Plot File Page Height” set the page size of the files, and “Clear all saved plots” empties the list. Tables and heatmap data can be saved in the same way. Tables saved with “Save to output”, for example the DEG data table, are listed under “Tables to Save” and are downloaded together as one Excel (.xlsx) file. Heatmap data saved with “Save GCT data file to output” in the Heatmap module (Chapter 6) or the WGCNA module (Chapter 9), or with the GCT buttons of the heatmaps in the Time Course Analysis module (Chapter 12), are listed under “GCT tables to Save” and are downloaded as GCT files, which can be opened in other tools such as Morpheus. In the example below, we saved the PCA plot, a volcano plot and a heatmap, the DEG data table, and the heatmap GCT file. 15.2 Save Session “Save Session” saves the current settings of all tabs, such as the selected groups and samples, comparisons, cutoffs and plot options, so that the same analysis can be continued later. Click “Save Session”, then click “Download Session File” to download the settings as a file; the file name starts with the project ID, followed by the date and time, for example Mouse_microglia_RNA-Seq_20261105_124611.rds. To continue later, open the same project and upload the file under “Restore Session from File”; Quickomics then restores the settings of all tabs. A session file can only be restored in the project it was saved from. If another project is open, Quickomics names the project that the file was saved for and asks Users to open that project first. Only the settings are saved: plots and tables saved to the Output tab are not included in the session file, so they have to be saved again after the session is restored. 15.3 Diagnostics The “Diagnostics” section at the bottom of the Output page helps to troubleshoot problems when running the application. “Log Level” (DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR) sets how much detail the session writes to the server log; the change takes effect immediately and affects only the current session. “Session Location” shows which server container is serving the session; please quote it when reporting a problem, as it identifies the log file to look at.
